description: The graph below shows average carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions per person in the United Kingdom, Sweden, Italy and Portugal between 1967 and 2007. Summarize the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

logical_frame.name: Introduction
logical_frame.value: The line graph compares four countries in terms of the amount of carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions per person per tonnes, measured in tonnes, between 1967 and 2007.

logical_frame.name: Overview
logical_frame.value: It is clear that the production of CO2 emissions in the United Kingdom and Portugal both declined while the opposite was the case for Italy and Sweden during the period shown. Additionally, out of four countries in the timeframe, the United Kingdom’s numbers were much higher in most of the years shown.

logical_frame.name: Body 1
logical_frame.value: Looking at the United Kingdom and Portugal, in 1967 the UK's emissions stood at approximately 11 tons per person, which was about 3 tonnes higher than Portugal's figure of 8 tons. Subsequently, the production of individual emissions in the UK declined steadily to around 8 tons by 2007, while Portugal's number rose to nearly 10 tons in 1977 before falling dramatically to approximately 5.8 tons by the end of the period.

logical_frame.name: Body 2
logical_frame.value: Regarding the remaining countries, in 1967, the amount of CO2 emitted in Italy was 4 tons per capita, which was more than double Sweden's figure of less than 2 tons. Thereafter, both countries saw consistent increases over the forty-year period, with Italy reaching roughly 8 tons and Sweden climbing to about 5.5 tons in 2007.

title: [12/08/2023] Employment patterns in the USA
description: The graph below presents the employment patterns in the USA between 1930 and 2010. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

logical_frame.name: Introduction
logical_frame.value: The line graph gives information about the proportion of American workers employed in various sectors from 1930 to 2010.

logical_frame.name: Overview
logical_frame.value: Overall, throughout the given period, the industrial, technical, and sales and office sectors emerged as major employers. In contrast, there was a sharp downward trend in the agricultural sector, falling from by far the most popular sector to the least by the end of the timeframe.

logical_frame.name: Body 1
logical_frame.value: Regarding industries that gained in popularity, in 1930, virtually no Americans were engaged in industrial and technical jobs, and only 10% pursued sales and office occupations. Thereafter, after having remained consistent until 1960, the industrial sector began attracting more workers, with its percentages rising gradually, ending up at its highest level of nearly 38% in 2010. Similar upward trends were also witnessed in technical and sales and office positions, as their participation rates underwent steady increases overall, to around 30% and 20% respectively in the final year, making them the second and third most common occupations.

logical_frame.name: Body 2
logical_frame.value: On the other hand, despite being the dominant industry in 1930, with approximately 75% of the labour force employed in farming, fishing and foresting, this sector saw a dramatic drop over the years, reaching a low of only 5% in 2010. Finally, the percentage of workers in other services rose from 10% to 15% in the first decade, then then fell back to a relatively stable level of around 10% for the rest of the period.

title: [Livestream 30/11/2024] Milk and butter
description: The table below illustrates weekly consumption by age group of dairy products in a European country. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

logical_frame.name: Introduction
logical_frame.value: The given table contains information about weekly dairy consumption of four age groups, namely below 25, 26 to 44, 45 to 64, and over 65, in a European nation.

logical_frame.name: Overview
logical_frame.value: Overall, it is clear that people of their retirement age drink the most milk, while those in the second oldest group eat by far the most butter. In addition, people across all age demographics prefer the low-fat alternative for both products, with the exception of the youngest group.

logical_frame.name: Body 1
logical_frame.value: Regarding milk consumption, people under 25 drink the least milk, at 1200ml per week, 59% of which is full fat, while the rest is low fat. 80% of the 1650ml drunk by those from 26 to 45 is low-fat milk, compared to 20% for full fat. Similarly, people in the second oldest age group drink 1670ml a week, at 55% for low fat versus 45% for full fat. 1900ml is drunk per week by the elderly, only 30% of which is full fat, while the remaining 70% is low fat.

logical_frame.name: Body 2
logical_frame.value: With regard to butter, while the youngest group preferred full-fat butter, accounting for 60% of the 12g eaten per week and 40% for low fat, the complete opposite was the case for those aged 26 to 45, at 38% for full fat and 62% for low fat of the 19g eaten. The amount of butter consumed by the second oldest age group is double that of the oldest one, at 60g and 30g respectively, with both groups consuming nearly equal amounts of full and low-fat butter.

title: [11/8/2024] Car ownership in the UK

logical_frame.name: Introduction

logical_frame.name: Overview
logical_frame.value: Overall, possession of automobiles in the UK increased over the thirty-year period, and having one car remained the most popular throughout the years.

logical_frame.name: Body 1
logical_frame.value: At the start of the period, similar proportions of people had one car and no cars, with figures of 45% and 43%, respectively. Thereafter, both options declined in popularity in the first decade. Over the next twenty years, the percentage of single-car ownership followed an upward trend, finally ending up at 45% in 2005. After falling from 43% in 1975 to 25% in 1985, the proportion of non-car owners continued to decline more steadily, and at the end of the period, 22% of individuals did not own a car.

logical_frame.name: Body 2
logical_frame.value: Regarding households with multiple cars, only about 6% owned two cars in 1975, while the figure for three-car ownership was negligible at roughly 2%. Both categories showed gradual increases over the next three decades, with two-car households rising to about 18% and three-car families reaching nearly 10% by 2005.

title: [19/8/2024] Women in the workforce

logical_frame.name: Overview

In addition, Sri Lanka and Japan maintain the largest gap between women's labour force participation and their representation in management roles.

logical_frame.name: Body 1
logical_frame.value: Regarding the three developed countries, women in the United States account for 46% of the workforce, which is 3% higher than the figure for those in managerial positions, at 43%. Female Australians constitute similar proportions in both categories, standing at around 43%. In contrast, 48% of the workforce in Japan are women, nearly triple the rate of those in managerial roles, at only 17%.

logical_frame.name: Body 2
logical_frame.value: Turning to the remaining nations, although 42% of workers in Sri Lanka are female, they constitute only 9% of management positions in that country, which is the lowest of the five listed. Similarly, a relatively large disparity is also seen in Egypt, as 20% of their labour force is comprised of women, nearly double the percentage of female managers, at only 12%.

title: [30/9/2023] The percentages of Chinese and Indian students in Canadian universities

logical_frame.name: Overview

In addition, the figures for New Brunswick were the largest in terms of both Chinese and Indian students, while no students from India chose P.E.I. as their place of study.

logical_frame.name: Body 1
logical_frame.value: Regarding the most popular destinations, New Brunswick took the lead, as it was comprised of roughly 12% and 7% Chinese and Indian nationals, respectively. A similar percentage of around 10.5% was seen in the figures for Chinese students in both Nova Scotia and British Columbia, while Indian students, in turn, accounted for just approximately 6.3% and 4.4%. Meanwhile, Quebec reported that slightly over 8% of their students were Chinese, which was about 2% higher than Indian citizens.

logical_frame.name: Body 2
logical_frame.value: As for the remaining provinces, in Alberta alone, students from India surpassed those from China, at approximately 5.5% and just above 4%, respectively. Additionally, the numbers of Chinese students in Yukon, Manitoba and Ontario ranged from slightly above 7.5% to as low as 6%, while Indian attendees came in at roughly 2.5% lower in all three provinces. Finally, Prince Edward Island was the only province with no reported students coming from India, although there remained slightly under 5% who were Chinese.

title: [Livestream 23/11/2024] Changes in annual spending by a particular UK school in 1981, 1991 and 2001

logical_frame.name: Overview
logical_frame.value: Overall, it is clear salaries made up the biggest proportion of each yearly budget, and teachers received the largest share collectively, while insurance was the least significant cost overall.

logical_frame.name: Body 1
logical_frame.value: Regarding the major components, teachers’ salaries accounted for 40% of the annual expenditure in 1981, half of the budget in 1991, and finally, 5% less than that figure in the final year, at 45% in 2001. This is three times higher than the amount going to the remaining staff at the school in 2001, which experienced a relative decline throughout the period, as the figure was initially up to 28% in 1981. Oddly, furniture and equipment spending stood at 15% in the first year, dipped by two-thirds to 5% by the next recorded period, before it regaining its position again, ultimately ending up at 23% in 2001.

logical_frame.name: Body 2
logical_frame.value: The portion of annual spending used for school resources, such as books, came in at 15% in 1981, but declined to only 9% in the next 20 years. This is in stark contrast to the insurance spending trend, which was gradually allocated more funding, rising fourfold from a negligible 2% to 8% in the final year.

title: [6/2/2023] The number of trips made by children in one country in 1990 and 2010
description: The chart below shows the number of trips made by children in one country in 1990 and 2010 to travel to and from school using different modes of transport. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

logical_frame.name: Introduction
logical_frame.value: The graph provides information about the number of trips to school made by different modes of transportation by children aged 5 to 12 in a particular country in 1990 and 2010.

logical_frame.name: Overview
logical_frame.value: Overall, there was a shift from active means of transport towards more passive ones, with walking being the most popular method in the former year, whereas car use became more preferred 20 years later.

logical_frame.name: Body 1
logical_frame.value: Looking at the main forms of transport, walking was the most popular mode with 12 million trips in 1990, three times higher than car passenger journeys at 4 million. However, walking trips halved to 6 million by 2010. In contrast, traveling by car saw a dramatic rise to 11 million trips by the end of the period.

logical_frame.name: Body 2
logical_frame.value: Regarding other modes of transport, cycling and combined walking and bus travel both recorded 6 million trips in 1990, while bus-only journeys were slightly higher at 7 million. Cycling witnessed the steepest decline, falling to just 2 million trips by 2010. Similarly, walking combined with bus use dropped to 3 million trips, while bus-only travel decreased more modestly to 5 million trips over the twenty years.

title: [27/12/2022] Factors affecting work performance of two age groups
description: The bar chart below shows the results of a survey conducted by a personnel department at a major company. The survey was carried out on two groups of workers: those aged from 18-30 and those aged 45-60, and shows factors affecting their work performance. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

logical_frame.name: Introduction
logical_frame.value: The given bar chart gives information on the different factors that influence work performance among two age groups, namely 18-30 and 45-60.

logical_frame.name: Overview
logical_frame.value: Overall, it is clear that the two demographics share similar opinions on the majority of factors; however, the younger group highly regards personal development, a relaxed work environment, job security, and promotion prospects, noticeably more so than the older group.

logical_frame.name: Body 1
logical_frame.value: Looking at the chart in more detail, the top concern for younger workers is having the chance to develop themselves, as 90% of them believe so, versus only around 40% of older workers agreeing. Promotion prospects and a relaxed work environment are the next two most important factors for workers under 30, being mentioned by 80% of them. By contrast, only half of the workers over 45 cite the former as a factor, and only a third of them bring up the latter.

logical_frame.name: Body 2
logical_frame.value: With regard to the remaining factors, money is the top concern for older workers, and fourth for younger ones, with roughly 70% of all workers surveyed mentioning it. 60% of workers in both groups also claim that team spirit is important, double the figure for the work environment among older respondents. Having job satisfaction, a competent boss, or respect from co-workers is cited by around 45% of all workers, with the older group placing a greater emphasis on the aforementioned factors, except for job satisfaction. Finally, 40% of younger employees want job security, which is double the figure for the older group.

title: [1/6/2023] Number of people per household in the UK in 1981 and 2001

logical_frame.name: Body 1
logical_frame.value: Starting with smaller households, in 1981, single-person households accounted for 17%, only half of those with 2 residents, at 31%. logical_frame.name: Body 2

These latter two categories saw decreases of 3% each, to 17% and 15% respectively. Larger households, specifically those with 5 and 6 individuals, also experienced a decline, falling to 6% and 2% respectively by the end of the period.

title: [Livestream 7/12/2024] Immigration from and emigration to a European country in 2009

title: [30/9/2023] - Fitness membership numbers across different age groups in an Asian country
description: The chart displays information about fitness membership numbers across different age groups in an Asian country from 1970 to 2000. Summarize the key information by highlighting the main features and make appropriate comparisons where relevant.

logical_frame.name: Introduction
logical_frame.value: The bar chart gives information about the numbers of fitness memberships among individuals of 3 different age groups from 1970 to 2000.

logical_frame.name: Overview
logical_frame.value: Overall, while fitness memberships of those from 18 to 35 displayed a trend of instability, those of people both under 18 and from 36 to 65 gradually rose over time. In addition, the young adult age group recorded the highest membership numbers for most of the given period.

logical_frame.name: Body 1
logical_frame.value: With regard to individuals in the 18-35 age group, its members numbered just over 2,000 in 1970. In the subsequent years, after an initial surge to 4,000 in 1975, membership receded to its original level of just over 2,000 in 1990. This was followed by another larger surge to a peak of 5000 members in 1995, before declining again to 4,000 five years later.

logical_frame.name: Body 2
logical_frame.value: As for the other two age groups, there were 1,000 members under 18 in 1970, double the figure for 36-to-65-year-olds. Thereafter, the number of gym members under 18 varied over the following 2 decades, from approximately 1,800 to 2,800, until 1990, when it began its ascent to a high of 3,500 by the end of the period. Likewise, membership among the oldest bracket also maintained a steady upward trend, but without any fluctuations, ending up at 2,700 in the year 2000.

title: [Livestream 28/12/2024] People from five European nations living in each other’s countries in 2011
description: The following table shows the number of people from five European nations living in each other’s countries in 2011. Summarize the information by selecting and reporting the main features and make comparisons where relevant.

logical_frame.name: Introduction
logical_frame.value: The table illustrates how many people from five different European countries resided in each other’s countries in 2011.

logical_frame.name: Overview
logical_frame.value: Overall, Britain and Germany were the two most popular destinations given to expatriates. In addition, Poland attracted the fewest people from the other four countries, while, in contrast, the total number of its citizens living in the other countries was the highest.

logical_frame.name: Body 1
logical_frame.value: Regarding the two most popular destinations, Germany was home to nearly 1.2 million expatriates, compared to over 1 million in Britain. In Germany, half of the immigrants were Italians, followed by Poles, with the respective figures of 556,000 and 426,000. Meanwhile, the number of British and Spanish residents amounted to slightly more than 100,000. In Britain, the Polish community was the largest immigrant group, numbering 550,000, nearly twice the size of the German one, at 297,000. In contrast, the figures for Spaniards and Italians residing there were significantly smaller, with populations ranging from 71,000 to 119,000.

logical_frame.name: Body 2
logical_frame.value: As for the other destinations, Spain ranked third, welcoming 861,000 immigrants from the listed nations, four times higher than Italy's 196,000. Spain was the preferred country for British immigrants, with 391,000, nearly twice the numbers of Germans and Italians (around 200,000 each), while only 86,000 came from Poland. In Italy, Poles were the predominant group (106,000), far outnumbering the other three nationalities, whose figures ranged between 19,000 and 42,000. Finally, the total number of expatriates residing in Poland was only 6,000, among which, more than two-thirds were from Germany, followed by modest British and Italian communities of around 700 people each.

logical_frame.name: Body 3
logical_frame.value: In total, there were 3.3 million expatriates from all five surveyed countries, with Poles constituting the largest group living abroad (1,168,000), followed by Italians, at 863,670. In contrast, the number of Spanish people opting to live outside their country was the lowest, at only 202,170. The figures for British citizens and Germans were comparable to one another, both exceeding 500,000.

title: [19/3/2022] Investment in funds of four categories from 1988 to 2014

logical_frame.value: The line graph displays trends in the values of four different investment categories in the United States between 1988 and 2014.

title: [C19T3] - The production of ethanol
description: The diagram below shows how a biofuel called ethanol is produced. Sumarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

logical_frame.name: Introduction
logical_frame.value: The diagram illustrates the cyclical process of manufacturing ethanol as a biofuel, from the initial growing of plants to the final product for transportation before being emitted to the environment.

logical_frame.name: Overview
logical_frame.value: Overall, this is a continuous cycle where carbon dioxide is both absorbed and released throughout various stages. The process consists of six main stages, beginning with plant growth and ending with ethanol being used for different modes of transportation.

logical_frame.name: Body 1
logical_frame.value: The process begins when plants and trees utilize energy from sunlight and carbon dioxide from the atmosphere to grow. These plants are then harvested using agricultural machinery before being transported to pre-processing facilities, where they are broken down into cellulose.

logical_frame.name: Body 2
logical_frame.value: In the following stages, the cellulose undergoes chemical processing to produce sugars, which are then fed to microbes. The resultant chemical compound is then processed to create ethanol, which is used to power various forms of transportation, including cars, trucks, and aircraft. Finally, through the combustion of of ethanol as a source of fuel, carbon dioxide is released back into the atmosphere, where it becomes available for plants to use again, thus beginning the cycle once again.

logical_frame.name: Body 1
logical_frame.value: In the first stages of the process, plastic bottles are collected in large wheeled containers before being transported to a recycling center by trucks. At the center, the materials are sorted to remove any unsuitable items. Following this, the sorted bottles are compressed into compact blocks, which are then crushed into smaller pieces.

logical_frame.name: Body 2
logical_frame.value: The latter stages of the process involve several transformations. First, the crushed pieces are washed before being processed into plastic pellets. After that, these pellets are then heated to be converted into raw material. Finally, this raw material is manufactured into various new products, including t-shirts, plastic bottles, and other items.

title: [26/02/2022] Wool production
description: The picture shows the process of making wool. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

logical_frame.name: Introduction
logical_frame.value: The diagram illustrates the sequence of steps involved in producing wool products from sheep.

logical_frame.name: Overview
logical_frame.value: The process consists of several stages, beginning with sheep rearing and culminating in the manufacture of end products.

logical_frame.name: Body 1
logical_frame.value: The process begins with the rearing of sheep, followed by wool shearing, where farmers remove the wool from the animals. The raw wool then undergoes a cleaning process to remove dirt and impurities. Following this, the wool is dried using specialized equipment, which prepares it for the next stage. Subsequently, the dried wool goes through a carding process, where it is combed and aligned, producing both tufts of wool and strings.

logical_frame.name: Body 2
logical_frame.value: While the strings can be recycled, the tufts of wool are placed in storage. After that, the stored wool undergoes yarn spinning, where it is transformed into balls of yarn. Finally, these balls of yarn can either be used for knitting or be made into finished products such as jackets or carpets.

title: [C20T4] - How bamboo fabric is made
description: The diagram below shows how fabric is manufactured from bamboo. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant

logical_frame.name: Introduction
logical_frame.value: The diagram illustrates the manufacturing process of bamboo fabric.

logical_frame.name: Overview
logical_frame.value: Overall, the production of bamboo fabric involves nine distinct stages, beginning with the cultivation of bamboo plants in spring and culminating in the creation of woven fabric. In addition, the process combines both agricultural and industrial techniques, requiring several months to complete from plantation to final product.

logical_frame.name: Body 1
logical_frame.value: The manufacturing process commences with planting bamboo plants during the spring season. After a growing period, the mature bamboo is harvested in autumn, when the plants have reached their optimal size. The harvested bamboo is then cut into strips using specialized cutting equipment, before being crushed to create a liquid pulp. This pulp undergoes a filtering process to separate the long fibres from the liquid component.

logical_frame.name: Body 2
logical_frame.value: The subsequent stages focus on refining and processing the extracted fibres. Water and amine oxide are added to soften the fibres, making them suitable for textile production. The softened fibres are then spun to create yarn, which serves as the raw material for fabric production. Finally, the yarn is woven together to form the finished bamboo fabric, completing the manufacturing cycle.

title: [06/01/2024] - Recycling paper
description: The diagram illustrates how recycled paper is made. Summarize the information by selecting and reporting the main features and make comparisons where relevant.

logical_frame.name: Introduction
logical_frame.value: The diagram illustrates the process by which used paper is transformed into recycled paper through a series of four main stages.

logical_frame.name: Overview
logical_frame.value: Overall, the paper recycling process involves four distinct phases: making pulp, filtering, cleaning, and producing the final recycled paper. The entire procedure transforms waste paper into a reusable product through mechanical and chemical treatment methods.

logical_frame.name: Body 1
logical_frame.value: The process begins with used paper being placed on a conveyor belt and transported to the pulp-making stage. During this initial phase, the used paper is mixed with water and chemicals in a large container to create unfiltered pulp. Subsequently, this unfiltered pulp undergoes a filtering process, where it passes through a filtering system that removes larger impurities and debris, resulting in filtered pulp.

logical_frame.name: Body 2
logical_frame.value: Following filtration, the cleaned pulp enters the cleaning stage, where ink and other contaminants are removed. This is accomplished through the use of an air pump system, combined with water and soap, which effectively eliminates ink particles to produce clean pulp. In the final stage, the clean pulp is processed through heated rollers with additional water to create the finished recycled paper, which can then be reused for various purposes.

chart_description:
TYPE: process diagram
TITLE: Recycled Paper Production Process
UNITS/AXES: Not applicable
SERIES/CATEGORIES:
1. MAKING PULP
2. FILTERING
3. CLEANING
4. PRODUCTION
DATA:
Stage 1: MAKING PULP
- Inputs: Used Paper, Water (H₂O), Chemicals
- Process: Used paper mixed with water and chemicals in a Mixing Tank to create Paper Pulp.
Stage 2: FILTERING
- Input: Paper Pulp
- Process: Pulp passes through a Filtering Machine to remove Impurities (Staples, Ink, Debris).
- Output: Filtered Pulp, Impurities (removed).
Stage 3: CLEANING
- Input: Filtered Pulp, Soap, Air (from Air Pump)
- Process: Air and soap are added to a Cleaning Unit. Ink floats off. Remaining particles are separated.
- Output: Clean Pulp, Ink (removed), Remaining particles (removed).
Stage 4: PRODUCTION
- Input: Clean Pulp
- Process: Pulp is pressed, dried, and smoothed on Heated Rollers over a Wire Screen to form Final Paper.
- Output: Paper Roll (new paper).
KEY FEATURES:
* The process begins with used paper being converted into pulp.
* The pulp undergoes two main purification stages: filtering and cleaning.
* Filtering removes solid contaminants like staples and debris.
* Cleaning specifically targets the removal of ink using air and soap.
* The final stage involves pressing, drying, and smoothing the cleaned pulp to produce new paper.
* The process is linear, moving from raw used paper to a finished paper roll.

logical_frame.value: The recycling process commences when used aluminum cans are deposited at collection centres, where they are stored in designated containers. This upward trend persisted throughout the following decades, with properties owned by occupants climbing to 59% in 1981 and 69% in 1991, ultimately peaking at 70% in 2001, though this figure subsequently fell back to 65% by the end of the period.

title: [C14T3] - Hydroelectricity generation
description: The diagram below shows how electricity is generated in a hydroelectric power station. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

logical_frame.name: Introduction
logical_frame.value: The diagram illustrates the process of generating electricity in a hydroelectric power station.

logical_frame.name: Overview
logical_frame.value: Overall, the electricity generation process involves multiple stages that operate differently during day and night cycles. The process begins with water stored in a high-level reservoir and ends with electricity being distributed to the national grid.

logical_frame.name: Body 1
logical_frame.value: During daytime operations, water flows from the high-level reservoir through the dam to the power station below. The intake system, which remains open during the day, allows water to flow downward and operate the reversible turbines. These turbines drive the generator to produce electricity, which is then transmitted through power lines to the national grid. Simultaneously, excess water continues flowing to a low-level reservoir located at the bottom of the system.

logical_frame.name: Body 2
logical_frame.value: At night, the process reverses to store energy for future use. The intake closes, and the reversible turbines switch to pumping mode, powered by electricity from the grid. Water is pumped from the low-level reservoir back up to the high-level reservoir, effectively recharging the system. This pumped-storage mechanism ensures continuous electricity supply by storing energy during low-demand periods and releasing it when needed during peak hours.

description: The diagram below shows two different processes for manufacturing black tea. Summarize the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

logical_frame.name: Introduction
logical_frame.value: The diagram illustrates two distinct manufacturing processes used to produce black tea, comparing traditional methods for making loose tea with modern techniques for creating tea bags.

logical_frame.name: Overall
logical_frame.value: Overall, both processes share identical initial and final stages, with the main differences occurring in the middle processing steps. While the traditional method involves rolling leaves to create loose tea, the modern approach uses cutting techniques to produce smaller granular pieces suitable for tea bags.

logical_frame.name: Body 1
logical_frame.value: The manufacturing process begins identically for both methods. First, only the bud and top leaves are carefully picked from tea plants to ensure good quality. These fresh leaves then undergo withering, where air is passed through them on racks, removing 60% of their moisture content.The processes diverge significantly in the next stage. In the traditional method, the withered leaves are rolled flat and broken, releasing enzymes from the leaves. Conversely, the modern method involves cutting, tearing and curling the leaves, which creates quick-processing smaller granular pieces rather than whole leaves.

logical_frame.name: Body 2
logical_frame.value: Both methods then follow identical final steps. The processed leaves undergo oxidation and fermentation, during which they are spread on tiles or cement surfaces. This stage causes the leaves to change to a copper color as enzymes react with air, developing flavor and aroma. Finally, the leaves are dried until 97% of moisture is removed, completing the black tea manufacturing process.

logical_frame.value: Upon arrival at the paper mill, the waste paper enters the cleaning stage, where it undergoes cleaning, pulping, and the removal of other materials such as staples. Subsequently, the paper moves to the de-inking phase, during which inks and glues are eliminated from the pulped material. Finally, the cleaned and de-inked pulp is fed into paper making machines, which manufacture usable paper products, thereby completing the recycling cycle.

title: [C12T4] - Understanding geothermal power generation
description: The diagram below shows how geothermal energy is used to produce electricity. Summarize the information by selecting and reporting the main features and make comparisons where relevant.

logical_frame.name: Introduction
logical_frame.value: The diagram illustrates the process by which geothermal energy is utilized to generate electricity in a geothermal power plant, demonstrating the transformation of cold water into electrical energy through underground thermal resources.

logical_frame.name: Overview
logical_frame.value: Overall, this is a linear process that harnesses the Earth's natural heat from hot rocks located deep underground to produce clean electricity. The system involves five distinct stages, from water injection to electricity generation, utilizing both underground thermal zones and surface-level mechanical equipment.

logical_frame.name: Body 1
logical_frame.value: The process begins with cold water being pumped down through an injection well to a depth of 4.5 kilometers below ground level, where it reaches the geothermal zone containing heated rocks. As the cold water comes into direct contact with these hot geological formations, it absorbs substantial thermal energy and transforms into hot water due to the intense underground temperatures. This heated water is then extracted back to the surface through a separate production well, bringing the absorbed geothermal energy to the surface level.

logical_frame.name: Body 2
logical_frame.value: Once above ground, the hot water is converted into steam, which then goes into a turbine where the steam's pressure and heat cause the turbine blades to rotate. This mechanical energy from the spinning turbine powers a generator, which converts the rotational motion into electricity. The generated electricity is subsequently transmitted through power lines for distribution to consumers.

title: [IELTS Trainer] - Manufacture of frozen fish pies
description: The diagrams below give information about the manufacture of frozen fish pies. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

logical_frame.name: Introduction
logical_frame.value: The diagrams illustrate the process of manufacturing frozen fish pies.

logical_frame.name: Overview
logical_frame.value: Overall, the production consists of multiple interconnected stages, beginning with the preparation of raw ingredients and ending with the freezing, storage, and final distribution of the finished product. Both potatoes and salmon are prepared separately in distinct processing lines before their ingredients are ultimately combined to create ready-to-eat pies for retail sale.

logical_frame.name: Body 1
logical_frame.value: At the initial stage, potatoes are delivered to the factory, where they are thoroughly cleaned, peeled, and sliced into smaller pieces suitable for cooking. These slices are then boiled, chilled, and carefully stored until required for later use. Meanwhile, fresh salmon is transported to the facility and must be processed within 12 hours of delivery to preserve its freshness. It is then cooked in a steam oven, after which the skin and bones are removed and discarded. In the next step, the remaining flesh is meticulously inspected to ensure that only high-quality portions are selected for the following phase.

logical_frame.name: Body 2
logical_frame.value: Following those preparatory stages, the prepared salmon will be mixed with peas, sauce, and the previously stored potatoes in microwaveable containers, which are sealed to create individual portions. After assembly, each pie is wrapped, labeled, and frozen at controlled temperatures to maintain its flavor and texture. Finally, the finished products are transferred to cold storage units, kept there until dispatch, and then delivered to retailers for public sale.

title: [IELTS Trainer] - Small-scale commercial honey production
description: The diagram below shows how honey is made in small-scale commercial production. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

logical_frame.name: Introduction
logical_frame.value: The diagram illustrates the process of small-scale commercial honey production, detailing the stages from initial nectar collection by bees through to the final packaging and distribution of honey for commercial sale.

logical_frame.name: Overview
logical_frame.value: Overall, the honey-making process comprises eleven distinct stages and is divided into two main phases. The first phase involves natural activities performed by bees within the hive, while the second phase consists of human intervention for processing and commercialization. The entire process begins with bees foraging for nectar from flowers and ends with packaged honey being sold to consumers.

logical_frame.name: Body 1
logical_frame.value: In the bee phase, worker bees first gather nectar from flowering plants and transport it back to their hive, where they deposit the honey. The bees then engage in drying the honey by fanning their wings over the cells while simultaneously keeping the cells clean. Next, the bees seal each cell with a protective layer of wax, preserving the honey.

logical_frame.name: Body 2
logical_frame.value: The human phase commences when beekeepers carefully gather the sealed honey combs from the hives. These combs are then subjected to pressing, which extracts the raw honey from the wax structure. Next, the extracted honey is transferred to a sump tank where it undergoes heating at temperatures ranging from 45 to 50 degrees Celsius. Subsequently, the heated honey flows through a sieve tank, where impurities such as dirt particles are removed. The filtered honey then moves to a settling tank, where it remains undisturbed for a period of two to four days. Finally, the purified honey is carefully poured into jars for packaging and loaded onto delivery vehicles for transportation and then sold to consumers.

logical_frame.value: Looking first at fixed telephony, subscription levels were about 1.7 per 100 in the mid-1990s and then increased steadily, moving above two by 1997 and reaching roughly 2.2 in 1998. logical_frame.name: Body 2

From 1999 onward, uptake accelerated, in which penetration reached one per 100 that year and then doubled to two in 2000. In 2001, mobiles matched and then surpassed fixed lines at about three subscribers per 100, before rapidly rising to nearly five in 2002, six in 2003, and close to nine per 100 inhabitants by 2004. title: [24/09/2025] Chipboard production and furniture manufacturing process
description: The diagram below shows how chipboards are created from wood and then used to make furniture. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

logical_frame.name: Introduction
logical_frame.value: The diagram illustrates the manufacturing process of chipboard from raw wood materials and its subsequent transformation into furniture items.

logical_frame.name: Overview
logical_frame.value: Overall, the chipboard production involves nine distinct steps organized into two main stages: preparation and production. The entire process commences with the harvesting of trees and culminates in the creation of finished furniture pieces, with the preparation stage requiring significantly more time than the actual production phase.

logical_frame.name: Body 1
logical_frame.value: The initial preparation stage encompasses five sequential steps. First, trees are cut down from forests, after which they undergo trimming to produce uniform logs. These logs are then fed into a specialized machine that converts them into small wood chips. Subsequently, the wood chips are subjected to a drying process using steam and hot air, which takes approximately 24 hours. Finally, the dried chips are stored for a period of one to two weeks before proceeding to the production phase.

logical_frame.name: Body 2
logical_frame.value: Turning to the production stage, it comprises four steps that transform the prepared wood chips into usable furniture. Initially, the stored chips are mixed with adhesive glue and wax to create a binding mixture. This mixture is then placed into moulds for shaping, followed by a pressing procedure that compresses the material into flat chipboard sheets. In the final step, these chipboard sheets are utilized to manufacture various furniture items, such as tables and chairs, completing the entire production cycle.

title: [YouPass Collect] - Olive Oil Production Process
description: The diagram details the process of producing olive oil. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

logical_frame.name: Introduction
logical_frame.value: The diagram illustrates the procedure for producing olive oil from harvested olives.

logical_frame.name: Overview
logical_frame.value: Overall, the process comprises several main stages: initial fruit collection and cleaning, mechanical oil extraction and final separation and storage of the products.

logical_frame.name: Body 1
logical_frame.value: Looking at the initial stages, olives are picked from the trees and deposited into collection vats where they are subjected to leaf removal and washing. Next, the cleaned fruit is transferred to an olive mill and crushed to form an olive paste. This paste then undergoes malaxation at temperatures below 27°C, a gentle mixing step that helps small oil droplets coalesce. After malaxation, the paste is directed into a centrifugal separator (centrifuge), where the bulk of the oil is mechanically extracted and separated from the solid material.

logical_frame.name: Body 2
logical_frame.value: From this stage onwards, the extracted liquid stream is subsequently treated to yield consumable oil and waste streams. Virgin oil is first transferred to a decanter for clarification, allowing solids and water to settle out. Any remaining liquid is passed through a separation stage in which residual wastewater is removed and either treated or discharged as effluent, while the purified oil is collected. The solid residue, or pomace, is removed from the centrifuge and transported for further refining or processing at specialist facilities. Finally, the clarified oil is deposited into a storage tank, ready for bottling or distribution.

logical_frame.name: Body 1
logical_frame.value: The production of all tea types begins with leaf growth, followed by plucking and wilting, also known as withering. Green tea, by contrast, requires two extra steps: the wilted leaves are first steamed and then rolled before being dried in the oven.

logical_frame.name: Body 2
logical_frame.value: The remaining three varieties all involve fermentation. For oolong tea, after wilting, the leaves are rolled and undergo slight fermentation before the final drying stage. The two black tea types follow a similar path but with full fermentation instead. The primary distinction between large leaf and small leaf black tea lies in their preparation method: while large leaf black tea is produced through rolling, small leaf black tea uses crushing to break down the leaves before fermentation and drying.

logical_frame.name: Introduction

logical_frame.name: Overview
logical_frame.value: Overall, the production of electricity from coal is a multi-stage process, beginning with the extraction of coal from a mine and culminating in the distribution of electricity to both commercial and residential buildings. Notably, waste heat is generated at two separate stages throughout the process.

logical_frame.name: Body 1
logical_frame.value: In the first stage, coal is extracted from an underground mine and transported to the surface in carts. It is then fed into a crusher, where it is broken down into smaller particles. The crushed coal is subsequently loaded onto trucks and delivered to a gasifier. At this facility, heat is applied to convert the coal into gas, which then moves to the next stage of the process.

logical_frame.name: Body 2
logical_frame.value: As for the remaining steps, the gas first enters a cooling facility, during which waste heat is released. Following this, it passes through a cleaning facility to remove impurities and other contaminants from the gas. The purified gas is subsequently fed into a gas power plant, where it is used to generate electricity, with additional waste heat being produced as a result. Finally, the electricity is transmitted via power lines to supply both commercial buildings and residential homes in urban areas.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

logical_frame.name: Introduction
logical_frame.value: The two bar charts illustrate the findings of a 2009 survey conducted in a European country, examining how frequently people replace their vehicles and what type of car they tend to purchase.

logical_frame.name: Overview
logical_frame.value: Overall, the data reveals that the majority of car owners in this country tend to keep their vehicles for extended periods rather than replacing them frequently. With regard to car purchases, second-hand vehicles were overwhelmingly the most preferred choice.

logical_frame.name: Body 1
logical_frame.value: Regarding car replacement habits, only a negligible proportion of respondents changed their car on a very frequent basis, with those doing so every year accounting for just 1%, while those replacing it every two years made up 5%. A considerably larger share, at 37%, upgraded their vehicle every three to four years. The single largest group, however, consisted of those who kept their car for five years or more, representing just over half of all respondents at 52%. Meanwhile, those who stated they never changed their car and those who owned no vehicle at all each accounted for a minor share, at 3% and 2%, respectively.

logical_frame.name: Body 2
logical_frame.value: Turning to car purchasing preferences, second-hand vehicles dominated the survey results, with 68% of respondents indicating they typically opt for pre-owned cars. In contrast, 25% of respondents preferred to buy new cars. Those who reported purchasing either new or second-hand depending on the situation constituted a modest 10%, while the proportion who did not own a car mirrored the figure seen in the first chart, at 2%.

title: [YouPass Collect] - International tourist arrivals comparison 2009-2010
description: The table compares the international tourist arrivals in millions in 9 countries in 2009 and 2010 and the changes (in percentages). Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

logical_frame.name: Introduction
logical_frame.value: The table illustrates the changes in visits from overseas to 9 countries, in both absolute and relative terms, in two consecutive years, namely 2009 and 2010.

logical_frame.name: Overview
logical_frame.value: Overall, with the exception of France and Hong Kong, all the countries welcomed more tourists in 2010. In addition, France was the most popular destination, while the most significant growth was seen in Germany.

logical_frame.name: Body 1
logical_frame.value: Regarding the most visited nations, in 2009, while 66 million people traveled to the US, Spain and the UK each attracted 55 million tourists, which was 11 million higher than Italy. An increase from 1 to 2 million was subsequently witnessed in these countries, equivalent to 1.5% to 3.6% growth. Meanwhile, France's number topped the list at 76 million in 2009, and remained unchanged in the following year.

logical_frame.name: Body 2
logical_frame.value: With regard to the remaining countries, the number of visitors to Turkey was 33 million, 11 million higher than that of China, which in turn outnumbered the next country, Germany, by the same margin. There was a rise of 12 million in the figures for all the 3 nations, with their relative growth being 33%, 55% and 109%, respectively. Hong Kong was the least appealing tourist destination, with its numbers declining from 10 to 9 million in 2010, representing a drop of 11%.

title: [YouPass Collect] - Time Spent by Students on Different Types of Websites

logical_frame.name: Introduction
logical_frame.value: The pie charts compare the proportions of time spent by male and female students on five different categories of websites.

logical_frame.name: Overview
logical_frame.value: Overall, there were notable differences between the two groups, with sport-related websites being the most visited by male students, whereas their female counterparts devoted the largest share of their time to study websites. Meanwhile, the proportion of time spent on other types of websites was identical for both genders.

logical_frame.name: Body 1
logical_frame.value: Regarding the categories with the most significant gender differences, sport websites attracted the highest percentage of male students' time, at 35%, which was more than three times the figure for females, at only 10%. Conversely, study websites accounted for 45% of female students' time, the single largest figure across all categories for either gender, compared to a considerably lower proportion of 30% for males. Additionally, female students spent four times as much time on shopping websites as their male peers, at 20% and 5%, respectively, representing the widest gap in relative terms.

logical_frame.name: Body 2
logical_frame.value: As for the remaining categories, male students allocated a fifth of their time to news websites, at 20%, which was 5 percentage points higher than the 15% recorded for female students, a relatively narrow gap compared to the categories mentioned above. Finally, both groups devoted an equal and relatively modest share of 10% of their time to other, unspecified website types, making it the only category where no difference between genders was observed.

title: [YouPass Collect] - Market share of three manufacturers of mobile phones: 1994 - 2004
description: The line graph below illustrates the proportion of mobile phone sales by three manufacturers (Motorola, Nokia and Sony Ericsson) between 1994 and 2004. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

logical_frame.name: Introduction
logical_frame.value: The line graph illustrates the market share, measured as a percentage of sales, of three mobile phone manufacturers, namely Motorola, Nokia, and Sony Ericsson, from 1994 to 2004.

logical_frame.name: Overview
logical_frame.value: Overall, the three brands showed distinct trends, with Nokia's market share rising significantly, Motorola's declining considerably, and Sony Ericsson's fluctuating within a narrow range. Notably, Nokia eventually overtook Motorola to become the dominant manufacturer for the majority of the period, while Sony Ericsson consistently remained the least popular brand.

logical_frame.name: Body 1
logical_frame.value: As for Motorola and Sony Ericsson, in 1994, the former held the largest market share at 32%, approximately three times higher than that of the latter, at just 11%. Motorola's figures then fell steadily over the following years, reaching a low of only 14% in 2000, before recovering slightly to 18% by 2004. Sony Ericsson, on the other hand, saw a modest rise, peaking at 15% in 1998, but then followed a similar downward path, dropping to 7% in 2003 before ending the period at 10%.

logical_frame.name: Body 2
logical_frame.value: Regarding Nokia, it began the period at 21%, making it the second most popular brand behind Motorola. Its share dipped slightly to 19% in 1997, before surging dramatically over the next five years to a peak of 37% in 2002, overtaking Motorola along the way. Despite this impressive growth, Nokia's market share fell back to 30% in 2004, though it still remained the leading brand by a considerable margin.

title: [YouPass Collect] - Cinema visits in Australia from 1996 to 2000
description: The graphs below show the cinema attendants in Australia and the average cinema visits by different age groups from 1996 to 2000. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

logical_frame.name: Introduction
logical_frame.value: The table and line graph illustrate cinema attendance rates and the average number of visits among Australians, along with a breakdown by four age groups, from 1996 to 2000.

logical_frame.name: Overview
logical_frame.value: Overall, while the percentage of the population going to the cinema rose and then remained steady, the average number of visits fell after 1997. Across all age groups, a similar up-and-down pattern was seen, with the 14-24 group consistently going to the cinema the most and the over-50s the least.

logical_frame.name: Body 1
logical_frame.value: In 1996, 62% of Australians went to the cinema, with each person visiting an average of 10.3 times. Both figures increased the following year, to 72% and 11.1 visits, respectively. From 1998 onwards, however, attendance stayed stable at between 70% and 72%, while the average number of visits dropped to 8.3 and remained at roughly this level until 2000.

logical_frame.name: Body 2
logical_frame.value: As for the age-group data, in 1996, the 14-24 group recorded 15 visits, followed by the 25-35 and 35-49 groups at 14 and 12, respectively, while the over-50s had the fewest at 10. All four groups rose and fell together, reaching highs in 1997 and 1999 and lows in 1998 and 2000. For instance, the youngest group climbed to 22 in 1997, dropped to 16 in 1998, peaked at 23 in 1999, then fell back to 18 in 2000. The other three groups followed the same pattern, with the 25-35, 35-49, and over-50 groups finishing the period at 17, 15, and 13 visits, respectively.

title: [YouPass Collect] - Satisfaction Levels of Full-Time and Part-Time Students About University Library Services
description: The charts below show the results of a survey conducted by a university library to find out the opinions of full-time and part-time students about its services. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

logical_frame.name: Introduction
logical_frame.value: The four pie charts illustrate the levels of satisfaction among full-time and part-time university students regarding two library services, namely IT support and opening hours.

logical_frame.name: Overview
logical_frame.value: Overall, while both student groups expressed high levels of contentment with the library's opening hours, opinions on IT support were far more divided, with part-time students being notably less satisfied. In addition, full-time students were generally happier with the services provided than their part-time counterparts.

logical_frame.name: Body 1
logical_frame.value: Regarding IT support, a clear majority of full-time students were very happy with this service, at 55%, compared to only a fifth of part-time students. Conversely, nearly half of part-time attendees reported being not at all satisfied, which was over three times higher than the figure for full-time students, at just 13%. Meanwhile, the proportion of students who were quite happy was relatively similar between the two groups, at 32% and 35% for full-time and part-time students, respectively.

logical_frame.name: Body 2
logical_frame.value: As for the library's opening hours, satisfaction levels were considerably higher for both groups. Approximately two-thirds and nearly three-quarters of full-time and part-time students, respectively, were very pleased with the current schedule. A further 32% of full-time students expressed moderate satisfaction, which was 9 percentage points higher than the corresponding figure for part-time attendees. Notably, dissatisfaction was minimal in both cases, with only 1% of full-time and 5% of part-time students reporting that they were not at all happy with this service.

title: [YouPass Collect] - European Medical Care Trends 1980-2000
description: The table shows information about medical care in three different European countries between 1980 and 2000. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features and make comparisons where relevant.

logical_frame.name: Introduction
logical_frame.value: The table illustrates the number of physicians and hospital beds per 1000 people, as well as the average length of hospital stays, in Austria, France, and Sweden over three years: 1980, 1990, and 2000.

logical_frame.name: Overview
logical_frame.value: Overall, while hospital beds increased across all three countries during this period, the figures for physicians and average hospital stays showed more varied trends. In addition, Sweden consistently led in most healthcare metrics throughout.

logical_frame.name: Body 1
logical_frame.value: Regarding healthcare resources, Sweden had the highest number of physicians in 1980 at 3.6 per 1000 people, followed by France at 2.4, while Austria recorded the lowest figure of 0.8. Over the next two decades, Sweden's figure fluctuated, dropping to 3.0 in 1990 before rising to 3.8 by 2000. Meanwhile, France declined to 1.3, and Austria increased modestly to 1.0. As for hospital beds, Sweden again topped the list with 6.4 beds per 1000 people in 1980, compared to 1.4 in Austria and 0.2 in France. By 2000, all three nations witnessed growth, with France dramatically rising to 1.6, Austria to 3.7, and Sweden to 6.9.

logical_frame.name: Body 2
logical_frame.value: Turning to the average length of hospital stays, Sweden recorded the longest duration at 23 days in 1980, significantly higher than Austria's 18 days and France's 9 days. France demonstrated a consistent downward trend, with the figure falling to 7 days in 1990 and 5 days in 2000, while both Austria and Sweden experienced fluctuations, ending at 18 and 21 days respectively.

title: [YouPass Collect] - Australian doctors: gender and origin trends
description:
The chart below gives information about doctors practicing in Australia over a 30-year period, including their gender and country of origin.
Summarize the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

logical_frame.name: Introduction
logical_frame.value: The table and bar charts give information about the total number of doctors in Australia, their gender composition, and their countries of origin across three time points: 1986, 1996, and 2006.

logical_frame.name: Overview
logical_frame.value: Overall, the medical workforce in Australia grew considerably over the 30-year period. While Australian-trained doctors consistently outnumbered their foreign counterparts, the gender balance among practitioners fluctuated noticeably throughout the cited period.

logical_frame.name: Body 1
logical_frame.value: Starting with the size and gender composition of the workforce, there were 300,000 doctors in Australia in 1986, with males accounting for a slight majority at 55% compared to females at 45%. The total figure rose sharply to 640,000 by 1996 before continuing to climb to 800,000 in 2006, more than doubling over the entire period. Regarding gender, a reversal was observed in 1996, when female practitioners edged ahead at 56%, while males fell to 44%. However, by 2006, males had regained the majority at 52%, with females making up the remaining 48%.

logical_frame.name: Body 2
logical_frame.value: Turning to the nationality breakdown, Australian doctors dominated the profession throughout, comprising 61% of the total in 1986, compared to 39% for those of other nationalities. This gap narrowed in 1996, when the share of Australian doctors dipped to 57% while foreign-trained practitioners rose to 43%. By 2006, however, the nationality ratio had returned to exactly its 1986 level, with Australian doctors once again accounting for 61% of the workforce and overseas-trained doctors making up the remaining 39%.

description: Many people today choose to have fewer children than their parents did. What are the reasons for this and what effects does it have on society?

title: Responsibility for Public Health
description: Some people believe that it is the responsibility of individuals to take care of their own health, while others think that governments have a greater role to play in protecting people's health. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
